name: Tātkālika
description: Bhāskara II's instantaneous motion of a planet, and why its velocity correction vanishes where the equation of centre is extreme.
aria: An epicycle model drawing a rosette, beside the equation-of-centre curve and its tangent
intro: In 1150 Bhāskara II asked how fast a planet moves at a single instant. The answer hides an idea we now call the derivative, and the rule that it vanishes at a maximum.
dock: <label class="chip">epicycle r/R <input id="kSel" type="range" min="5" max="80" value="32" style="width:90px;accent-color:#ff8a3d"></label>
legend: mean planet: moves at constant speed
E(M): the correction over one lap
tangent turns green where the rate is zero

tutorial.b: In the Indian model, an imaginary mean planet goes round the earth at a steady speed (gold, on the big circle). The true planet rides a small circle, an epicycle, around it (white). So sometimes the real planet runs ahead and sometimes it lags.
tutorial.see: the labels: earth, mean planet, true planet.

tutorial.b: True place = mean place + a correction E, the equation of centre. E depends on M, how far round the epicycle the planet is. The purple curve on the right is E over one full lap.
tutorial.see: the dot on the purple curve moving as the planet goes round.

tutorial.b: Bhāskara II (1150) separated average daily motion from the speed at an instant: tātkālika gati. It's the slope of E right now, the tangent line on the curve. True speed = mean speed × (1 + dE/dM).
tutorial.see: the tangent line, and 'true speed / mean speed' in the readout.

tutorial.b: At M = 90° the correction is at its largest and the tangent is flat: the rate of change is zero. Bhāskara notes the mean speed is exact there. Today we write it as f′(x) = 0 at a maximum.
tutorial.see: the tangent turning green and flat, and dE/dM = 0.

tutorial.b: The green bead knows nothing but the slope where it stands. It steps uphill, a little at a time, and always stops where the slope is zero. That's gradient ascent, the same idea used to train every neural network.
tutorial.see: the green bead settling at the top of the curve.

tutorial.b: A bigger epicycle means a bigger correction, a steeper curve and a wilder rosette. The rosette is just the orbit drawn from a slowly turning viewpoint; the physics doesn't change.
tutorial.see: the taller purple curve. Try 'epicycle 0.15' for a nearly circular orbit.

sound:
The pitch is the planet's speed. Every 0.7 seconds a note plays whose height is 4 × (true speed ÷ mean speed). When the planet runs fast the note is high; when it lags, low. Over one lap you hear the speed rise and fall like the purple curve's slope.

The bowl rings at the instant dE/dM = 0, the extreme, where true speed equals mean speed.

Every chamber plays in Raag Bhupali: five notes, Sa Re Ga Pa Dha, tuned as whole-number ratios of the home note Sa (138.6 Hz here): 1, 9/8, 5/4, 3/2, 5/3. Simple ratios mean the sound waves line up every few cycles, so they never clash. That lets the math pick any note it likes and it still sounds like music. Underneath, a tanpura drone holds Sa and Pa, and a bansuri improvises in the same raag. The santoor and the singing bowl are the ones the math plays.

faq.a: Bhāskara II's term for a planet's speed at a single instant, as opposed to its average daily motion. In modern terms it's a derivative.
A small circle (radius r) whose centre moves round a big circle (radius R). The planet rides the small one. Here r/R sets how lopsided the motion is.

faq.q: what is the equation of centre?
faq.a: The correction added to the mean position to get the true one: E(M) = −arcsin((r/R)·sin M).
It's an early form of the derivative and of the rule that it vanishes at an extremum, about 500 years before Newton and Leibniz, but without their general theory.
A gradient-ascent climber: it only knows the instantaneous slope dE/dM and keeps stepping uphill with a bit of momentum. It always stops where the slope is zero.

faq.q: why is the orbit a flower?
faq.a: It's drawn from a frame that turns a little slower than the mean planet, so each lap lands slightly rotated. Only the viewpoint turns; the motion is the same.
Bhupali uses five notes, Sa Re Ga Pa Dha, tuned as the ratios 1, 9/8, 5/4, 3/2 and 5/3. It has no half-steps, so any note the math picks sounds consonant against the drone.

Sa is 138.6 Hz. Every other note is Sa times a whole-number ratio (9/8, 5/4, 3/2, 5/3) or that times a power of 2 for higher octaves. Which note plays is chosen by a number in the scene. Open 'why this sound' to watch it live.
The haze behind the math is a kaleidoscope shader. Its symmetry follows the chamber's math, but it's decoration. Say 'trip 0' to switch it off and see only the math.
Isha Maini, a data science student at Emory. Each chamber's math is written and tested in Python and JavaScript before it's drawn.
